final_formulas.formula: (Na + K + Li + Rb + Cs + 2*(Ca + Sr + Ba)) / (Al + 0.0001)
final_formulas.name: inorganic_cation_to_al_charge_ratio

descriptor.assumptions: Assumes (i) gel Al mole fraction tracks the framework Al content achievable, which fails for gels where Al is not incorporated (e.g., F-/Ge or purely siliceous systems) or where P/Al phosphates dominate; (ii) inorganic cations are the only alternative charge compensators (hydroxide/fluoride roles ignored); (iii) divalent Ca/Sr/Ba count at full 2+ equivalent even though their structure-direction differs from alkalis; (iv) the 0.0001 denominator constant makes the ratio explode for Al-free gels, which tree splits can still handle but effectively treats all Al-free gels as equivalent at the high end. The formula ignores framework charge from other heteroatoms (B, Zn, Ga).
descriptor.expected_effect: As the descriptor increases beyond ~1-2, probability mass should shift from OSDA-templated high-silica frameworks (MFI, *BEA, MTW) toward alkali-templated low-silica frameworks (LTA, FAU, CHA) and, at extreme values, toward Failed. As it decreases toward or below 1, OSDA-dominated frameworks and all-silica-type products should become more likely.
descriptor.falsification: If phase selectivity is unchanged across a wide range of the ratio, or if low-silica frameworks (LTA, FAU) are obtained at ratios near or below 1 while high-silica frameworks appear at very high ratios (opposite of predicted ordering), the charge-density-mismatch hypothesis is contradicted for this dataset.
descriptor.formula: (Na + K + Li + Rb + Cs + 2*(Ca + Sr + Ba)) / (Al + 0.0001)
descriptor.hypothesis: The ratio of inorganic cation charge equivalents to the trivalent T-atom (Al) content of the gel acts as a proxy for the charge-density mismatch between the inorganic cations available to balance framework negative charge and the anionic charge generated by Al incorporation. Gels where this ratio is low require the OSDA (or hydroxide-mediated defect chemistry) to carry most of the charge compensation, favoring high-silica, OSDA-templated frameworks (e.g., MFI, *BEA, MTW). Gels where this ratio is high have ample inorganic cation charge to compensate framework Al at low Si/Al, favoring alkali-templated low-silica frameworks (e.g., LTA, FAU, CHA, SOD-like phases) or interzeolite-conversion-style products, and extreme values may push toward Failed/dense phases when charge density is far from any framework's matchable range.
descriptor.mechanism: Each framework Al introduces one negative charge that must be balanced by an extra-framework cation (inorganic or organic). The inorganic cations (Na+, K+, Li+, etc., counted with their valences) compete with the OSDA for this role. When inorganic cation charge greatly exceeds the charge that framework Al can generate, the excess alkali acts as an inorganic structure-directing agent and mineralizer, steering crystallization toward the small-pore, low-silica cages (sodalite, LTA, CHA, KFI-type) that accommodate clustered alkali cations and water, as in OSDA-free/seeded beta and K-nitrate-rich ZK-5 routes. When it is scarce relative to Al, the OSDA charge density must match the framework charge, gating which topology crystallizes; if neither cation pool matches, the gel stays amorphous or yields dense phases. Tree ensembles can split directly on this single charge-balance column, which is otherwise only implicit in combining many D0 columns.
descriptor.name: inorganic_cation_to_Al_charge_ratio

descriptor.assumptions: Uses F as a proxy for HF-derived fluoride and sda1 for total monocationic OSDA charge; assumes OSDA1 is the dominant organic cation (ignores OSDA2/3, captured only weakly by n_osda), that F- remains available (not volatilized or precipitated) during crystallization, and that formal charge of the OSDA is +1 (osda_charge exists but multiplying by it would require abs(osda_charge); keeping the simple ratio preserves interpretability). Gels without OSDA are pinned near 0 by the 1e-4 constant, which conflates them with hydroxide-route gels; those cases are partially disambiguated by the existing inorganic_cation_to_al_charge_ratio descriptor.
descriptor.expected_effect: As the ratio increases from 0 toward ~1: probability of high-silica defect-grown phases (*BEA, MTW, ISV/BEC, UTL) rises and Failed outcomes among OSDA-only gels fall. As the ratio increases beyond ~1 into excess-fluoride territory: probability shifts toward D4R/cage-containing frameworks (CHA, LTA, AEI, LEV, BEC) and, in Ge-bearing gels, toward D4R-rich phases; heteroatom-poor small-pore products replace Al/B-incorporating ones. Very low values (near 0) with high OSDA and low Al should raise Failed/competing-phase (FER, MFI) probabilities.
descriptor.falsification: If held-out publications show that product phase is essentially invariant to F/sda1 while varying other parameters (i.e., fluoride amount merely tracks sda1 in this corpus), or if high-silica OSDA gels with F/OSDA << 1 routinely crystallize defect-balanced frameworks rather than failing or switching phases, the charge-counterbalance mechanism behind the descriptor is falsified.
descriptor.hypothesis: The molar ratio of fluoride to OSDA1 in the gel is a phase-selectivity switch that is not available to the classifier from F and sda1 independently, because tree ensembles cannot form their ratio. Three regimes should map to different product families: (i) F/OSDA near 0 (hydroxide/mineralizer-dominated media, F present only as a trace) favors Al-incorporating, charge-balanced frameworks directed by inorganic cations plus OSDA at higher pH (e.g., MFI, MOR, FER, TON, AEL, or Failed under overly basic conditions); (ii) F/OSDA around 1 (classic equimolar fluoride route) favors high-silica, large-pore frameworks grown at low pH where each single negative framework charge or connectivity defect is counterbalanced by one OSDA cation (e.g., *BEA, MTW, ISV/BEC, UTL); (iii) F/OSDA substantially above 1 (excess fluoride) promotes encapsulation of F- in small double-four-ring (D4R) cages and competes with trivalent heteroatom incorporation, favoring small-cage and D4R-rich frameworks (e.g., CHA, LTA, AEI, LEV, and Ge-containing D4R phases such as BEC/UTL) while narrow-composition windows can tip toward Failed or competing phases (e.g., FER, RUT-like byproducts).
descriptor.mechanism: In fluoride media the pH is low and silicate species are highly condensed; each OSDA+ must be charge-balanced either by one [AlO4/2]- or [BO4/2]-/tetravalent-heteroatom-associated charge or by one F--stabilized connectivity defect (SiOSi...F-). When F is deficient relative to OSDA and the gel is Al-free, the OSDA cannot be neutralized by defects and crystallization stalls (amorphous/Failed) or shifts to Al-bearing competing phases; with equimolar F, defect-charge-balanced high-silica frameworks become accessible; with excess F, F- is preferentially occluded in D4R units (whose negative charge it balances internally), stabilizing cage/D4R-rich topologies and suppressing heteroatom uptake. This is exactly the HF/OSDA phase-selection behavior demonstrated for beta vs. ZSM-5 vs. amorphous outcomes (evidence 2) and the excess-fluoride ERS-7/PST syntheses where F/OSDA > 1 uniquely opens narrow windows for new small-pore phases and F/OSDA <= 1 gives FER (evidence 3).

descriptor.assumptions: (i) A single apparent activation energy (Ea/R = 9000 K) is a reasonable proxy across all gel chemistries; real Ea varies with OSDA, mineralizer and gel composition, so the descriptor is an approximation that only ranks thermal severity within a moderate temperature window (roughly 80-200 °C; the exp() argument stays in a numerically safe range there). (ii) It assumes time-temperature equivalence, i.e., that the phase evolution depends on the integrated rate, not on sequential events such as heating ramps or seeding, which the record does not capture. (iii) It ignores supersaturation/dilution effects (item 10 shows H2O/SiO2 co-determines the Beta/ZSM-12 switch), so this descriptor is complementary to, not a replacement for, composition-based dilution measures. (iv) For records with extreme temperatures far outside typical windows the extrapolated rate factor may be unreliable.
descriptor.expected_effect: As the thermal dose increases, yields of kinetically trapped, low-framework-density phases (FAU, *BEA, MWW, ISV/BEC, LTA) should fall, while higher-stability phases (MTW, MOR, TON, MFI at high dose) and over-ripened dense/amorphous outcomes labeled Failed should rise; intermediate doses should maximize the metastable large-pore phases.
descriptor.falsification: If the held-out performance of the classifier is unchanged or degraded when this descriptor is added, or if predicted phase labels show no systematic trend with the descriptor (e.g., FAU/*BEA appearing as often at high thermal dose as at low, or MTW/Failed appearing at the lowest doses), the Arrhenius-combined time-temperature control hypothesis is contradicted. It would also be falsified if cryst_time and cryst_temp interact sub-Arrhenius (e.g., phase outcomes depending on temperature thresholds alone regardless of duration), meaning a piecewise temperature term, not a dose integral, is the relevant quantity.
descriptor.hypothesis: A single 'thermal dose' — crystallization time weighted by an Arrhenius factor for a typical zeolite crystallization activation energy (~75 kJ/mol, Ea/R = 9000 K, referenced to 423 K so the descriptor equals the actual time at 150 °C) — controls where a synthesis sits on the kinetic-to-thermodynamic phase-selectivity axis. Syntheses with low thermal dose (short times or modest temperatures) arrest metastable, kinetically favored, lower-framework-density phases, whereas high thermal dose (long times and/or high temperatures) lets the system ripen toward thermodynamically more stable, higher-framework-density phases or dense byproducts. Because trees split on one column at a time, the classifier cannot combine cryst_time and cryst_temp into this joint kinetic quantity and must instead learn disjoint thresholds on each, which generalizes poorly across publications that trade time against temperature.
descriptor.mechanism: Zeolite crystallization proceeds through successive nucleation and solution-mediated dissolution/reprecipitation (Ostwald ripening). The rate of both T-atom redistribution (dissolution of less stable frameworks and growth of more stable ones) and heteroatom reorganization follows an Arrhenius dependence on temperature, so time * exp(-Ea/RT) is the natural integrated measure of how far the solid-liquid system has progressed toward equilibrium. Metastable, open frameworks (e.g., FAU, *BEA, MWW-type lamellar precursors) nucleate fast at high supersaturation but redissolve once the mother liquor equilibrates; frameworks of higher stability/density (e.g., MTW/ZSM-12-type, MOR, analcime-like dense phases) dominate at large thermal dose. In fluoride media the Beta-vs-ZSM-12 switch under Ostwald ripening is driven exactly by temperature, time and dilution-controlled supersaturation, and in hydroxide media FAU converts to NaP/analcime-like phases with rising temperature or time.
descriptor.name: thermal_dose_cryst_time_x_arrhenius
